title_en: I've played GTA 6 on Xbox Series S: How Does the Weakest Console Handle the Biggest Game of All Time?
summary_en: GTA 6 is finally here, and one of the biggest questions heading up to launch is how well the Xbox Series S would handle the game – well, I've finally had the chance to play the game on the tiny Xbox.
body_en:
GTA 6 is finally here , and one of the biggest questions heading up to launch is how well the Xbox Series S would handle the game – well, I've finally had the chance to play the game on the tiny Xbox.
Rockstar announced a couple weeks ago that all versions of GTA 6 would be 'targeting' 30 fps , and while it's disappointing that even the PS5 Pro won't be able to hit 60 fps, that performance is about what I expected from the Xbox Series S. And while I wait for my framerate analysis to stop running on my first clip of the game, the Xbox Series S version actually seems pretty decent, all things considered.
The Xbox Series S obviously doesn't have the same graphics treats that the PS5 Pro version of the game has, but even without the ray traced shadows and the PSSR, the game holds up well on the 1440p machine. Character models are still extremely detailed, and even has some decent subsurface scattering and the environments are incredibly beautiful, no doubt learning from Rockstar's time with Red Dead Redemption 2.
But where the Xbox Series S falls short is in the finer details. The edge of nearly every surface is aliased, almost looking like there's a border of static around every character and building, particularly around people's hair. There's also an early scene on a boat, where Jason's face is noticeably soft until it zooms closer in, no doubt to save on some GPU resources. But, GTA 6 on the Xbox Series S is using FSR 4 to upscale from 720p up to 1080p, according to Wccftech , so some softness is to be expected.
The game just went live, and I'm waiting for the framerate analysis to finish on my initial clip of the game (it takes a minute,) but just going off of my gut, it feels like a smooth 30 fps, even on the Xbox Series S. However, it does feel like the game drags occasionally, especially when swapping between scenes, but again that's something that I'll be able to confirm once Trdrop finishes doing its thing.
I didn't get early access to GTA 6, so all of this is based on the first section of the game. The real test of GTA 6's performance is going to be how it handles some of the wild scenes that are sure to come in the later parts fo the game. But, any action game needs to nail the calmer moments if it wants any chance of standing up when you're surrounded by explosions and gunfire, and when it comes to GTA 6 on the Xbox Series S, it mostly nails that baseline. The game looks great, considering the level of hardware available, but you will definitely notice the difference if you put it side-by-side with something like the PS5 Pro.
As GTA 6's launch unfolds, we'll be live blogging the game , watching for all the weird and wild stuff that the community finds. IGN also gave GTA 6 a perfect 10, where reviewer Luke Reilly calls it "exquisitely detailed, endlessly ripe for experimentation, and uncompromisingly engineered, Grand Theft Auto 6 is the single most impressive video game I have ever played. " For everything else GTA 6, stay tuned to IGN.
Jackie Thomas is the Senior Tech Editor at IGN and the PC components queen. She's been covering gaming hardware for more than a decade for IGN, TechRadar, Gizmodo, PC Gamer and more. You can follow her  @Jackiecobra
